Overall I think this pack is a little bit weaker than the last few but definitely not the worst and is still worth it in my opinion. Ill rank these games from my favorite to least favorite. However I might rank some games higher than I like them since how I rank them is my opinion, and then the ranking is what I think of it as whole for everyone.

Starting off is Job Job. This one was really tough since personally I don't think this is that great of a game actually, for me and my group we are really a bunch of bozos and we seem to have a really hard time finding the right words to accurately answer the prompt in a funny way. However this is in no way a bad game at all, this game is really fun but I think it just takes the right group. The way I see this game is that it is just basically Quiplash when you choose the words from other peoples answers from the icebreaker question. So good game, but Quiplash is just better. This one is a low A tier for me.

Next up is Weapons Drawn. This might be one of my favorite "not funny" Jackbox games of all time meaning that the purpose of it is not to be funny but something else. Basically in this game you are given a letter from your name and you have to fit that letter into a drawing that you make of a predetermined weapon, you do this two times and then one of those that you drew will be the weapon that you dropped for the rest of the game (used for people to compare murder weapons to to see if the letters match). Then you come up with a name for a guest and then when it comes to the murdering part, you pick a guest and guess who brought them, if you get it right you kill them successfully. Finally you see the weapon that a person was killed with and try to match that weapon with the weapon that all of the people dropped at the beginning of the game revealing whether they were the murderer or not. Overall this is probably one of the most complicated jackbox games of all times and because of that I think you really need the right group of people and you 100% need the time to learn it which might take a few games that could last very long. Luckly for me, I had the perfect group of people and after we took the time to learn how to play, we had a blast playing this game. For me this is S tier but objectively this is probably a solid low B or high C.

Coming up next is Poll Mines. This game I think will be great for any group of people. Its not too long, its a great bit of fun since you have to work in teams of two. And is great for teamwork and strategizing with friends. Not to much to add, you basically get a prompt and have to rank the answers which creates a general ranking for each answer, than the teams take turns discussing what order the answers are in based on the round. Ex: "Rank top 3" "Rank worst to best" or "Rank 2, 3, and 4". Overall this game is great but can get boring if played too much so I would say an objective rating of 8/10 or around a solid mid B.

Drawful Animate is next and while we had a lot of fun with this one, the other ones were just better for our group personally. This game is like any other game of drawful but you instead have to make two slides that loop to make a small animation with your prompt. You can also double up for when you are almost 100% sure you have the right answer. This game for us was like maybe a 6/10 but I think objectively this is definetly top 2 with Job JoB coming in with an A.

Last and also least is The Wheel Of Enormous Proportions. This was not only the worst one for our group but also objectively this one just kinda falls short. I wont go too much into this one but basically its a trivia game thats not just multiple choice thats also mixed with complete RNG with spinning a wheel deciding who gets points. depending on how you look at it, it can either seem like a good concept with horrible execution or horrible concept with a great execution. I have to give it at least a little bit of credit since it does have a great visual design and has a pretty solid narrator. This one is a not-so-solid 5/10 or D tier both subjectively and objectively for me.

Overall, this pack is pretty good but definitely not as good as the as previous games, (especially after pack 7 which in my opinion was the best pack by a long run.) Overall a B tier game. Definitely worth it if you have other packs, but if its your first pack i would go with pack 7 or maybe 6 depending on what you want.

The Jackbox Party Pack 8 continues the franchise’s tradition of delivering quick, quirky, and socially-driven mini-games perfect for parties, streams, or casual get-togethers. Developed by Jackbox Games, this eighth entry maintains the formula of bundling five distinct games into a single package, each one leveraging humor, creativity, and crowd participation as core gameplay elements. While the collection doesn’t radically reinvent the franchise, it introduces fresh mechanics and a couple of standout titles that make it a worthwhile addition to the ever-growing Jackbox catalog.

The pack opens with Drawful: Animate, a clever evolution of one of Jackbox’s most popular drawing games. As the name suggests, players now draw two-frame animations instead of static images, adding a layer of creativity and absurdity that enhances the already chaotic charm of the original. The added movement makes it easier to communicate certain ideas—and, ironically, even easier to misinterpret them—resulting in a constant stream of hilarious guesses and moments of shared confusion. It’s a strong start to the pack and arguably the highlight, especially for players who enjoy drawing games and visual humor.

The Wheel of Enormous Proportions is the second title in the pack and brings a game-show aesthetic with a quirky, mystical theme. Players answer trivia questions to earn spins on a giant, colorful wheel that determines points, power-ups, and occasionally dramatic twists of fate. The presentation is slick, with a talking, sarcastic wheel that injects personality into the game. While it leans more on chance than some other trivia games in the series, it manages to balance knowledge and luck in a way that keeps it fun for players of all skill levels. However, the game can drag a bit, especially with larger groups, as wheel spins and animations take time to resolve.

Job Job is a standout concept that leans heavily into absurdist humor. Players respond to job interview prompts using words pulled from other players’ previous answers, creating weird, jumbled, and often hilariously broken responses. The fun here lies in how ridiculous the resulting sentences can be and how well players use the mess of words to craft convincing or comedic replies. It taps into the same energy as games like Mad Libs or Quiplash, but with a more structured framework. Job Job benefits from strong writing and an understanding of comedic timing, making it one of the most original and memorable entries in this pack.

The fourth game, The Poll Mine, introduces a more strategic, team-based experience. Players rank answers to a given prompt in secret, then work with teammates to guess the collective order as they explore a dark cave. It’s a mix of social deduction and puzzle-solving, and it rewards insight into group psychology more than traditional trivia or creativity. The visual style and thematic presentation are engaging, with a dungeon-delving flair and a sense of progression that builds suspense. Still, The Poll Mine may not land as well with groups unfamiliar with each other, as much of the enjoyment relies on accurately predicting group preferences.

Rounding out the pack is Weapons Drawn, a deduction-heavy murder mystery game where everyone is both killer and detective. What makes it unique is that players must draw their weapons—literally—incorporating a letter from their name into the drawing. The twist is that you leave your weapon behind at the crime scene, and others must deduce whose weapon it was based on the drawing. It’s clever, layered, and ambitious, though the rules and mechanics take some time to grasp. Inexperienced groups may find it harder to follow, and like some other deduction games, it’s best enjoyed with players who are invested in unraveling the puzzle rather than rushing through.

From a technical standpoint, Jackbox Party Pack 8 follows the familiar and accessible format: one device hosts the game, and all participants join via browser on phones or tablets. This ease of use continues to be a major strength of the series. The games are well-optimized, load quickly, and offer helpful options like moderation, audience participation, and content filters. That said, the overall visual design, while polished, is starting to show its formulaic structure across packs. Each game has its own theme, but there’s a clear aesthetic consistency that could start to feel repetitive to long-time players.

What Jackbox Party Pack 8 does well is variety. Whether your group prefers trivia, drawing, wordplay, or strategy, there's something here to enjoy. The balance between creative expression and structured gameplay is well-maintained across the collection, and games like Drawful: Animate and Job Job inject enough innovation to keep things fresh. Still, the pack doesn’t feel as universally strong as some earlier entries—there’s no single game with the breakout potential of Fibbage, Quiplash, or Tee K.O., but several solid experiences that depend on group chemistry to truly shine.

In conclusion, The Jackbox Party Pack 8 is another dependable entry in a long-running series known for its social, offbeat fun. It brings enough new ideas to entertain returning players, while remaining accessible to newcomers. While not every game hits the same high note, the overall collection is strong, particularly with the creative highs of Drawful: Animate and Job Job. It’s not the most essential pack in the series, but it’s a worthy addition for party game enthusiasts and a reliable go-to for a fun, laughter-filled night with friends or stream audiences.

Party Pack 8 demonstrates that the Jackbox team only gets better and better each and every year. Just like the pack preceding it, Party Pack 8 is chock-full of substantial and entertaining games, each one pretty considerably wonderful.

Job Job is one of the best games that has ever been released in a Party Pack. One of the few that my group has been able to consistently return to night after night, play for literal hours at a time, and continue to want to play. The highlight of this pack, far and away. Make sure you fill your icebreakers near the character limit; the game is much more fun with more words to work with!

I really enjoyed Poll Mine personally; it's like a much more personal take on Guesspionage (one of my personal favorites from Party Pack 3). The group is surveyed in various categories, and you need to guess what aggregate ranking certain choices got in the whole group; depending on the friends you play with, this can be an absolute treat.

Drawful: Animate is more of the same from the Drawful series, but that's never a bad thing; given drawful was going on half-a-decade without a new iteration (!!!) it was a welcome return of a series classic. The animation gimmick is lovely and the prompts are updated to be even more closer-to-the-pulse-of-modern-internet-slang, so sometimes we've been fooled by prompts being close enough to things my friends actually say that it was indistinguishable from someone aiming to get the likes award. Really fun, as drawful tends to be!

Weapons Drawn is a heavy time investment, but absolutely warrants the time spent by providing pretty hilarious gameplay. Some people get really creative with hiding their weapons! It's impressive how many ways you can hide a cursive "t". Sort of a better take on Push the Button, and I'm a big fan of it for being a better deductive reasoning game (though PtB has its upsides, too.)

The Wheel of Enormous Proportions is... well, my group isn't a fan. It seems like it's trying to be Trivia Murder Party (zany trivia with consequences for getting questions wrong, but getting a question wrong isn't the end of the game), but while the killing floors in TMP are interactive and interesting, the wheel spins really leave the fate of this game up to RNG - this makes it unrewarding to be good at the trivia (bad rng can equalize the playing field to an unreasonable degree) while also being boring to those not skillful at trivia (sure, you're not out of the game, but hoping on wheel spins to get back into the game is about as interesting as if every death in TMP was decided by the loser wheel. Yawn!) Ultimately, probably the lowest point of the pack - not a terrible game, just not Jackbox's greatest trivia showing. 

Ultimately, Party Pack 8 is one of my personal favorites in the storied series of party packs - a high recommendation from me!

For context, I own all of the Jackbox packs from 3-7 (as they are all of the good ones), and I wanted to get this pack as it looked as solid as the ones from before.

Weapons Drawn looked like an interesting murder mystery, with Job Job and Drawful Animate looking like good ones for laughs.

However, as I soon to find out, this pack wasn't as good as I was led to believe.

[u]Drawful Animate:[/u]

Honestly, a pretty solid one. The problem however arose when the prompts given were incredibly obscure things, leaving many people to draw random things like an Among Us guy, leaving the answer to be extremely clear and obvious, ruining the game. 

This problem could just be with the concept of Drawful itself, however when you do get a non-obscure prompt, it can be a fun time. However, when you do get a non-obscure prompt, it can be explained and drawn usually in one frame, with use of a second pretty much useless. 

The only good you get out of the 'Animate' part of this one is through the images you draw for your characters, which says a lot.

2.5/5

[u]Wheel of Epic Proportions:[/u]

On the surface, a normal trivia game, but once you dig deeper, it is quite bad. Like Trivia Murder Party, the questions are fairly obscure, however, this game isn't 'who can search on google the quickest', because even if you get every question right, this game is completely chance based. 

That's right, and the points system is even more messed up when it comes to the part where points can be split, and instead of it being done evenly, the majority of the points go to the person with lesser points, making both players have a similar amount of points, making the game even less fun.

2/5

[u]Job Job:[/u]

This game is pretty solid, but nothing legendary by any means. It tries to imitate much better games like Survive the Internet or Quiplash, and it does it well enough in that regard. Many say this one is the best, but I think it's tied with Poll Mine, which I'll talk about next.

4/5

[u]Poll Mine:[/u]

Poll Mine honestly is a pretty okay game, which I did enjoy. The only flaw with this one is the fact that usually during Jackbox you're in a room or voice call with the rest of the other players, meaning the other team can hear you discussing, and if you were to move room or voice call, then the other team will be unable to see what the other team had picked, giving them a disadvantage.

This means when a team says that either the answer is A or B, and when you pick one of them and get it wrong, it leaves the other team able to pick the the other option, making them win in the end.

This could be completely intentional by the developers, and it probably is, but for me it just does ruin the experience, however it is still a fun game.

3.5/5

[u]Weapons Drawn:[/u]

Weapons Drawn was actually the game I was most interested in. The concept of everyone being both a Detective and Murderer was interesting, to say the least, but unfortunately the game was ruined for a number of reasons.

First of all, the game was too complicated, at least according to my friends. I understood the game, but my friends said that they had no clue what they were doing the entire time. And in a sense, it's true. 

The drawing game where you had to guess the killer via a letter from their name would've been fine on it's own, but on top of that it was added with accomplices and guessing who is partnered with the accomplices, which is completely unnecessary and unlinked to the core concept of the game.

Secondly, since players can see other players votes, people will usually just follow the herd and vote whoever is being voted by someone else. At times, it is completely unclear whether or not you're supposed to discuss and point out who the killer is, as if you do, once again, other players will herd the person and get the points alongside you, but even if you don't tell anything, other players will assume you know what you're doing, and vote alongside you, once again getting points with you.

Third, it is strange that the letters the game pick's out of your name isn't specifically the first or last one, but instead it's a random one from your name, at least that is what it seems to be. The game no longer is about skill (like the wheel), but it's about who has the most convenient name, who has the longest name, and if RNG is on their side.

Fourth, once you catch a killer, they continue to play the game. Though I guess it's wise to be against throwing out a player mid-game for losing, however, isn't that the entire point of a murder mystery?

1/5

[u]Conclusion:[/u]

Jackbox 8 is the weakest pack out of the one's that I currently own (3-7), and though I can tell they tried hard with these games, they just aren't the best, especially with the price being a lot higher than the other ones. Jackbox 3 and 4 still stand as the greatest entries at such a lower price, but this game has only two fairly good ones, with 4 of them being flawed in some way, and Weapons Drawn being so flawed I had to write 6 paragraphs to explain that fact.

With the current price, Jackbox 8 isn't worth it. It's fun for a single session, but it gets pretty old fast. Definitely get Jackbox 3-7 first, then wait for this one to go on discount once the next couple ones come out, because, don't get me wrong, this is still a brilliant party game, but just not the most strong one.

Easily one of the weakest entries in the series. 7 was really damn good, but there's barely any reason for me to return to 8 overall. Weapons Drawn was the only one that I'd bother to ever replay. Then you vote on who you think is a killer and once you've done that, you will not learn if you received points or not. Too much for a game that's supposed to be a fun title for a fun night.

I could go into more detail as to why I think this is one of the frustrating entries in the series, but you really should not get this pack unless you have more than 4 people to play it with.

Technically you can play 80% of the games with 3 players, but games like Poll Mine were clearly not designed for small crowds even if only 2 people are needed to play it.

Quick Game by Game review:
Drawful Animate is hurt by the fact that you can't erase anything and that the actual drawing experience was a lot better in the previous Jackbox pack's drawing game Champ'd Up
Wheel of Enormous Proportions: This game had the potential to be the next Trivia Murder Party and could have carried the pack by itself with a better balance between luck and rewarding the contestants who actually know the answers to the trivia questions. The trivia portion of the game is as solid as any entry Jackbox has put out, but starting every player off with two slices to put on the wheel was a mistake. I don't know why Jackbox hasn't put out a patch to at least give players the option to make it less luck based.
Job Job: I loved it, but the group I played it with did not.
Poll Mine: This game is good. It's better with a larger group (as are most Jackbox games). However, in this case it's especially important based on the game mechanics
Weapons Drawn: STEEP learning curve. If you can get past that, then I think this game has the most potential as it combines a lot of the elements that make Jackbox games fun into a single game. My group got bored and wanted to go back to Trivia Murder Party after 3 games of it and we've never gone back.

In conclusion: There are stronger Jackbox packs out there (especially 6 and 7) and most of them are a lot cheaper as well. Also, I'd highly recommend skipping this pack entirely if the group of people you're going to be playing it with is 4 or fewer.

The Jackbox party pack 8 is one of the worst packs in the series. I do not understand the positive reviews for it - I can only assume that the individuals rating this game have stayed isolated since the beginning of COVID and have not actually played it in a group setting.

To start with, the wheel of enormous proportions is quite possibly the worst game ever made in the Jackbox franchise. It single handedly has killed the vibe of every group I have played it with. Drawful Animate is likely the best game in the pack, however also falls quite flat. It is a shell of other popular multiplayer "animate" games, but was fun about once. 

Poll Mine is not the worst mini-game, however it just doesn't have the spark that many of the previous packs bring to the series. With limited chances to be creative, have any spontaneity, the game becomes rather boring quickly.

We are now on the eighth iteration and seeing as how 7 was easily one of the best, this one had a lot to live up to.

[b]Note: Trimmed review to fit character limit, check video for full version![/b]

[h2]Drawful Animate[/h2]
Drawful Animate has some good ideas – create a simple two-frame animation and pit it against a bunch of possible answers – but the underlying “animate” mechanic just falls flat. A lot of the time, the phrase given can be demonstrated in just one drawing, no animation required.

That and a lot of the prompts are just boring or use super obscure language that even I needed to google to make sure I knew what I was drawing. It can be fun at times with the right group, but honestly, you’re probably better off just playing Gartic Phone, which has a much better animation game mode. This one just felt like Drawful with an unnecessary extra step – a waste of a game for a new Party Pack.

[h2]The Wheel of Enormous Proportions[/h2]
You’re basically tasked with solving trivia and spinning a wheel in hopes that your score can get up to 20k. Problem here is that both the trivia and wheel spinning are just straight RNG. It does not even matter if you know the trivia or not, a lot of the time you can simply put in whatever answers and get enough points to spin the wheel and even if you are not spinning it yourself – another player is spinning it with the chance of getting you points.

And once you do get to that 20k points, you’re given ANOTHER wheel to spin to determine the winner amongst ALL players with 20k points. The game is effectively RNG layered on top of more RNG and the trivia stuff feels underutilized as a result. It was really disappointing as a fan of trivia games and even though I do like myself some RNG, this one just doesn’t cut it.

[h2]Job Job[/h2]
As if to balance out the two duds so far, Job Job comes out of nowhere and cements itself as not only the best game of the pack, but one of the best games in ANY Jackbox Party Pack. The game revolves around answering questions about a potential job and using other players’ own words to compose entirely new sentences. The result is often chaotic, deadpan, or just straight-up hilarious. Depending on the group, the prompts can bring out some really interesting answers to work with and the fact that you can pull words from the questions themselves is a cool bonus too.

It’s simple concepts like these that Jackbox Party Packs really excel at and it’s perhaps the most accessible in the pack too, anybody can hop in and understand what to do without needing a big tutorial beforehand. It is for this game alone that I will likely keep the Party Pack installed for.

[h2]The Poll Mine[/h2]
This one is a step up in complexity, but it’s got a really neat concept. You play in teams and your goal is basically to guess the group consensus on certain questions and rank the different answers provided.

The team focus adds this entire new layer to the gme, as you want to discuss with your team what the right answer may be, but doing so in a way that doesn’t give enough info away to the other team to use if your team gets it wrong – as the other team picks up right where you left off. It’s a neat tug-of-war concept that’s only aided by its absolutely absurd prompts, like “what is a smell you only want to sniff once and never again”. Easily the second-best game in the pack.

[h2]Weapons Drawn[/h2]
On one hand, the concept is really neat. You have to draw “weapons” but must include a letter from your name so that when you kill a target, other players can attempt to deduce who the murderer was. On the other hand though, that is just one aspect of this game and there are a couple other layers that elevate it beyond the simplicity one would usually expect from a Party Pack title.

In a way, this kinda defeats the spirit of the series, as it is not one you can just pop open during a party without expecting at least a few players to be confused and ruin the gameplay for the others. Once you get over that hurdle, it can be fun, but it takes a bit to get there and it doesn’t help that games last a long time. I’d place it as my third favorite in the pack, but I can’t say it’s one I’ll be returning to much.

[h2]Overall[/h2]
Party Pack 8 is a bit of a letdown following the release of the excellent Party Pack 7. The overall pack is less consistent, has only one real standout, and is perhaps the weakest in the series yet (I have played from 4 onwards). Job Job may have carried it a bit, but that is likely the only game in the pack that will be getting plays from my group in the future, even if Poll Mine and Weapons Drawn aren’t all that bad.
